title: Early Magnetic Resonance Detection of Natalizumab-Related Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy in a Patient with Multiple Sclerosis
case_prompt:
A 44-year-old man with a 12-year history of relapsing–remitting multiple sclerosis had been treated with interferon until June 2009 and then started on natalizumab because of worsening gait dysfunction. In December 2011, he noted progressive memory and concentration deficits and experienced episodes of verbal aggression, mood changes, and suicidal thoughts. He was admitted for evaluation.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was performed on a 3.0-T scanner, including T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, diffusion-weighted imaging, post-gadolinium T1, and single- and multivoxel proton spectroscopy. Imaging showed a large, irregular subcortical lesion in the semioval center beneath the left frontal lobe with minimal involvement of subcortical white matter of the right hemisphere and the anterior commissure. The lesion was hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR images, hypointense on T1-weighted images, showed no contrast enhancement after gadolinium administration, and no restricted diffusion. Proton spectroscopy demonstrated elevated lactate and myoinositol levels and an increased choline peak with reduction of creatine and N-acetyl-aspartate in both mono- and multivoxel spectra.

On the basis of these findings, natalizumab was discontinued and a lumbar puncture was planned.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary CNS lymphoma was considered but imaging lacked the typical contrast enhancement and diffusion restriction seen in lymphoma—“Primary CNS lymphoma … characterized at MRI by intermediate-to-low signal intensity on T1-weighted images, and either isointense or hypointense signal on T2-weighted images, restricted diffusion, typical homogeneous CE and elevated lipid peaks and Cho/Cr ratio on MRS.”
2. Ischemic infarct was considered but the lesion did not conform to a vascular territory or show perfusion abnormalities—“Ischemic infarct … at MRI as an area of hyperintensity on FLAIR sequences after 6 hours from onset, abnormally perfused on PWI and with increased lactate and decreased NAA on MRS.”
3. Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis was considered but lesions in ADEM often ring-enhance and demonstrate variable restricted diffusion—“ADEM may appear … at MRI as multiple areas of hyperintensity at the gray-white matter junction demonstrating variable restricted diffusion and a possible ring enhancement.”
4. EBV-induced encephalitis was considered but typically shows diffusion restriction and increased myoinositol and choline, without the extended white-matter pattern—“CT in EBV induced encephalitis … at MRI by restricted diffusion and increased myoinositol and choline.”
5. Toxoplasmosis was considered but lesions usually present with ring enhancement, edema, and elevated lactate and lipids—“Toxoplasmosis … on T1- and T2-weighted images with ring enhancement, edema, elevated lactate, and lipids at MRI.”
6. Early-stage brain abscess was considered but abscesses characteristically restrict diffusion centrally and show succinate or acetate peaks—“Early-stage brain abscess … at MRI … characterized by restricted diffusion and elevated succinate and acetate on MRS.”
7. MS relapse was considered but active demyelinating plaques typically enhance after gadolinium and do not exhibit the same spectroscopy profile—“MS relapse … by high signal lesions on T2-weighted and FLAIR images that are enhanced when active on T1-weighted images after Gd administration … with decreased NAA on MRS.”
